## Design a Config Management / Feature Flag System

> **Core Concept:** This is a system that gets to be less reliable than nothing else in the entire company: every service that depends on it treats a flag check as a near-free, **always-available local call**, so the actual hard problem isn't storing a boolean, it's building a config-distribution pipeline that is ==more available than every single system that will come to depend on it==.

### Problem Statement
Design a feature flag and configuration management system: engineers
define flags and config values, target them to specific users or a
percentage rollout, and every running instance of the application, across
millions of client devices and thousands of servers, picks up changes
quickly, evaluates targeting rules locally, and keeps working even if the
flag service itself is unreachable. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: How quickly does a config change need to reach every running instance, seconds, or is a minute or two of propagation delay acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Sub-second propagation to millions of clients pushes toward **persistent connections** (streaming/websockets) with real fan-out infrastructure. A looser bound allows simple periodic polling, which is dramatically simpler and cheaper to build and operate, so this single answer decides the whole delivery mechanism.

#### Q: What happens to a service if it can't reach the flag system at all, does it fail open, fail closed, or use a cached last-known value?
*Why it matters:* Since this system sits in the request path of everything that checks a flag, its own downtime must ==never become everyone else's downtime==. The answer decides whether every SDK needs a local, persisted cache of the last known configuration to keep evaluating correctly even fully disconnected.

#### Q: What kinds of targeting do we need, simple on/off, percentage rollout, or rules based on user attributes (segment, region, plan tier)?
*Why it matters:* Simple on/off is a single boolean lookup. Attribute-based targeting rules require the **evaluation logic itself** (not just the raw flag value) to be shipped to every client, since evaluating 'is this user in the 10% rollout bucket for their account' has to happen locally without a network round trip.

#### Q: Do we need audit history and instant kill-switch rollback for a bad config change?
*Why it matters:* A bad flag change (a targeting rule that accidentally enables a broken feature for 100% of users) needs to be reversible in seconds, which means every change must be **versioned** and a rollback must propagate through the exact same fast distribution path as a forward change, not a slower out-of-band process.

### Functional Requirements
- An engineer can create a flag or config value, and update it (on/off, a percentage rollout, or targeting rules) through an admin interface or API.
- Every running instance of the application (client SDKs and server processes) can evaluate a flag's current value for a given user/context, locally and quickly.
- Config changes propagate to all running instances within a defined time bound, without requiring those instances to restart or redeploy.
- The system supports percentage-based rollouts and targeting rules based on user/account attributes, evaluated consistently for the same user across repeated checks.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- The system must be ==more available than every service that depends on it==: a flag check must never become a hard failure for a caller, even during a full outage of the flag system's backend.
- Flag evaluation latency must be **near-zero** (sub-millisecond, effectively a local lookup), since flag checks happen extremely frequently, often on hot request paths.
- Config changes must propagate to the large majority of running instances within seconds to a couple of minutes, so operators can trust a kill-switch actually reaches production quickly.
- The same user must get a **consistent evaluation result** for a given flag across repeated checks and across different service instances, so a user doesn't flicker between 'feature on' and 'feature off' mid-session.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Flag evaluations per second:** 500,000 requests/sec * 5 flags/request = **2.5 million evaluations/sec**, which must be served locally (no network call), since even 1ms of added latency per evaluation at this volume would be unacceptable
- **Full config payload size and initial sync cost:** 10,000 flags at ~200 bytes each (rules, percentages, targeting) = ~2 MB total config; 100,000 instances each need this on startup, ≈ 200 GB of initial-sync payload, small enough to serve from a CDN-backed cache rather than a live database
- **Update fan-out load per change:** 200 changes/day, each needing to reach 100,000 instances: with a streaming push model that's 200 * 100,000 = 20 million push notifications/day (≈230/sec average, bursty around deploy times), trivial compared to the 2.5 million/sec local evaluation load
- **Polling alternative fan-out load:** If instead every instance polled every 30 seconds instead of a push model: 100,000 instances / 30 sec = ~3,300 poll requests/sec sustained, every second of every day, just to catch changes that happen 200 times/day, which is why ==push beats poll== once instance count is this high

*Summary:* Evaluation volume (2.5 million/sec) so dramatically dwarfs change volume (200/day) that the entire architecture is built to make evaluation a pure **local, in-memory, network-free operation**, and to make distributing the rare change cheaply and quickly the only real network-facing problem, which is exactly why local SDK caching plus a push-based update stream, not a live network call per evaluation, is the design.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A polling model has every instance periodically ask 'has anything changed' on a fixed interval, simple and stateless on the server side, but forces a trade-off between propagation speed and load: a short interval catches changes fast but multiplies request volume by instance count, a long interval reduces load but delays how fast a kill-switch actually takes effect. A push model has every instance hold open a **persistent connection** (SSE or a long-lived streaming RPC), and the server proactively sends a diff the instant a change is published, **decoupling propagation speed from instance count** entirely, at the cost of the server needing to maintain many concurrent open connections and a fan-out mechanism.

#### undefined
Because a flag check is expected to be an effectively free, always-available local call, the SDK evaluates entirely against its own in-memory (and disk-persisted) cache of the last known config rather than calling out to the backend on every check. This means the config service's own uptime does not gate the uptime of every dependent service: if the backend is fully down, or the network between an instance and it is partitioned, the SDK simply keeps using its last-synced config, which is **stale but still correct** as of the last successful sync, rather than the calling application breaking or blocking.

#### undefined
A percentage rollout (say, 10% of users) can't be a ==coin flip evaluated fresh on every check==, since that would make a feature flicker on and off for the same user between requests, a confusing and sometimes state-corrupting experience. Instead, the SDK **deterministically hashes** a stable identifier (typically user ID plus flag key, so a user's bucket differs per flag) into a fixed range (say 0-9999), and compares that hash against the rollout percentage's threshold; the same input always produces the same hash, so the same user consistently lands on the same side of the line for a given flag, every time, on every instance, with no coordination or shared state needed between instances at all.

lesson.content:
## Design a Content Moderation System

> **Core Concept:** The core tension isn't detection accuracy, it's **throughput allocation**: there are always vastly more posts than human reviewer-hours, so the entire system is really a **triage and prioritization engine** that decides which tiny fraction of content a human ever looks at, and ==getting that ordering wrong== (reviewing a spam post before an active violent threat) is a worse failure than any individual misclassification.

### Problem Statement
Every piece of content posted to the platform (text, images, video) needs
to be checked against content policy before, or shortly after, it becomes
visible to other users. Design the system that screens billions of posts a
day: automated classification, a human review queue for anything the
machine isn't confident about, prioritization so the worst content gets
human eyes fastest, and an appeals process for users who think they were
moderated unfairly.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the volume of content per day, across which content types (text, image, video), and how fast does a human review pipeline need to keep pace?
*Why it matters:* Video moderation (needs frame sampling, transcription) is a fundamentally heavier pipeline than text moderation (near-instant classification). The mix of content types decides whether the ML layer can be one shared service or needs to be specialized per content type.

#### Q: Does moderation need to happen before content is visible (pre-publish, blocks the post) or after (post-publish, content goes live immediately and is pulled down later if flagged)?
*Why it matters:* Pre-publish moderation adds latency to every single post (including the 99.9% that are fine) and creates a hard bottleneck the write path can never outpace. Post-publish moderation keeps posting fast but means some bad content is briefly visible before removal, a trade-off with real product and legal implications.

#### Q: How is 'severity' defined, is a self-harm threat treated the same urgency as mild spam, and who decides that ranking?
*Why it matters:* Without a severity model, a human review queue is just FIFO, and FIFO is actively dangerous here: an urgent, high-harm report sitting behind ten thousand queued spam reports is a real-world failure, not just an inefficiency. This decides whether the queue is a simple list or a priority structure.

#### Q: What's the false-positive tolerance? How costly is it to the business/users if the ML layer wrongly auto-removes legitimate content?
*Why it matters:* A model tuned for high recall (catch everything bad) will also over-flag legitimate content, which is exactly why an appeals workflow and a human review layer exist at all rather than trusting automated classification outright. This decides the ML layer's confidence thresholds for auto-action versus queue-for-review.

### Functional Requirements
- Every piece of newly posted content is automatically scored by an ML classifier for policy violations across multiple categories (spam, harassment, violence, nudity, misinformation, etc).
- Content the model is highly confident about (either clearly fine or clearly violating) is auto-actioned (published normally, or auto-removed) without human involvement.
- Content the model is uncertain about is placed in a human review queue, ordered by a computed priority/severity score, not simply by arrival time.
- A human reviewer can view flagged content with context and issue a decision (approve, remove, escalate), and a user whose content was removed can file an appeal that routes to a (different) human reviewer.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- The ML classification step must add negligible latency to the post-publish path (well under a second) so moderation doesn't become the bottleneck for the far larger volume of ordinary, non-violating content.
- The system must sustain throughput of billions of moderation decisions per day without the human review queue growing unboundedly, meaning auto-action rates must handle the overwhelming majority of volume.
- High-severity content (credible threats, imminent harm) must reach a human reviewer within minutes, not hours, even during queue backlog, which requires the queue to support true priority ordering, not just FIFO.
- The moderation and appeals pipeline must produce an auditable trail (what was flagged, by which model version, reviewed by whom, what decision and why) for policy accountability and legal requirements.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Content requiring ML classification:** 500,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 5,800 items/sec average that must pass through the ML pipeline, this is the number the classifier's inference infrastructure must sustain continuously
- **Volume landing in the human review queue:** 500,000,000 * 5% = 25 million items/day requiring human review
- **Human reviewers needed to keep the queue from growing:** 25,000,000 items / 500 items per reviewer-shift ≈ 50,000 reviewer-shifts/day; even across a large global follow-the-sun workforce, this is a huge, expensive number, and it's the number that forces the auto-resolution rate to be as high as possible
- **High-severity items needing sub-minutes response:** 25,000,000 * 2% = 500,000 urgent items/day ≈ 5.8/sec average, small in volume but each one needs to jump the entire queue, which is why priority ordering (not FIFO) is non-negotiable

*Summary:* The single fact that drives this architecture is that **human review capacity** is the scarcest resource by orders of magnitude (50,000 reviewer-shifts a day just at a 95% auto-resolution rate), so every design decision, from confidence thresholds to priority scoring, exists to protect that scarce resource and spend it on the highest-severity 5% that actually needs a human.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A plain FIFO queue treats a barely-over-the-line spam post posted a minute ago as more urgent than a credible violence threat posted five minutes ago, purely because it arrived first, which is exactly backwards from what actually matters. Priority needs to be computed from severity (how bad, per the ML model's category confidence), potential reach (a post from an account with 10 million followers vs 10), and freshness decay (an old unactioned item should slowly gain priority so nothing starves forever).

#### undefined
The ML classifier doesn't output a binary answer, it outputs a confidence score per policy category. Somewhere between 'definitely fine' and 'definitely violating' there's a zone of uncertainty, and where you draw the two threshold lines (below which auto-approve, above which auto-remove, in between queue for human review) directly trades off human workload against both false positives (removing legitimate content) and false negatives (leaving violating content up).

#### undefined
A human reviewer processing hundreds of decisions a day is itself a point of failure, whether through fatigue-driven inconsistency, bias, or in rare cases deliberate abuse of moderation power. The system needs mechanisms to detect and bound the damage from any single reviewer's mistakes without slowing down the overwhelming majority of correct decisions.

## Design a Coupon/Discount System

> **Core Concept:** A coupon code is really a **shared counter** with a hard ceiling, and the entire design problem is making sure thousands of customers racing to redeem the same popular code at the same moment can never push that counter past its cap, which is a ==concurrency problem== wearing a discounts costume.

### Problem Statement
Design a coupon and discount system for an e-commerce checkout: a customer
enters a coupon code at checkout, the system validates it (is it real, is
it expired, has this customer already used it, has it hit its global
redemption cap) and applies the discount. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Does a coupon have both a global usage cap (e.g. 'first 10,000 redemptions') and a per-user cap (e.g. 'once per customer'), or only one of those?
*Why it matters:* A per-user-only cap is a simple keyed lookup against that one customer's redemption history. A global cap under high concurrency is the harder problem, since it requires coordinating a single shared counter across every concurrent checkout in the system, which changes the storage and locking strategy entirely.

#### Q: Can multiple coupons be stacked on a single order, or is it strictly one coupon per checkout?
*Why it matters:* Stacking means validation has to check compatibility rules between coupons (some combos allowed, some explicitly excluded), not just validate one code in isolation, which adds a rules-evaluation layer on top of simple cap checking.

#### Q: Is a coupon's validity based purely on its expiry date, or can it also be restricted by product category, minimum cart value, or specific SKUs?
*Why it matters:* Pure expiry-date validation is a cheap timestamp comparison. Category or SKU-scoped restrictions mean the validation step has to inspect actual cart contents against the coupon's rule set, which is a materially heavier check that has to happen on every checkout attempt, not just once.

#### Q: If a coupon redemption succeeds but the overall order later fails or is cancelled, should the coupon usage be automatically released back?
*Why it matters:* If yes, redemption isn't final until order confirmation, which means the system needs a reservation-then-confirm flow (similar to inventory) rather than a single atomic decrement, directly shaping whether redemption count is decremented eagerly or held provisionally.

### Functional Requirements
- A customer can enter a coupon code at checkout, and the system validates whether it's currently valid (exists, not expired, not yet at its usage cap).
- The system enforces a global redemption cap on a coupon (e.g. 'only the first 10,000 uses succeed') without ever allowing more redemptions than the cap.
- The system enforces a per-user redemption cap (e.g. 'each customer may use this code at most once').
- A valid coupon's discount is correctly applied to the order total before payment is charged.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Coupon validation must be fast, well under a couple hundred milliseconds, since it sits directly in the checkout critical path.

## Design a Delivery Route Optimization System

> **Core Concept:** This is a computational problem wearing a distributed systems costume: the optimal ordering of N stops is **combinatorially explosive** to compute exactly, so the real design decision is which **approximate heuristic** to run, how much time to give it, and how to re-run it fast enough to react to a route that's already in progress.

### Problem Statement
Design a system that takes a driver's set of assigned delivery stops for
the day and produces an efficient order to visit them in, minimizing total
drive time. New orders can be added mid-route, so the system must be able
to re-optimize a route the driver is already partway through. Design the
system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: How many stops does a typical route have, and how many drivers are we optimizing for simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* The traveling-salesman problem is **NP-hard**: exact solutions are feasible for maybe 10-15 stops but become ==computationally impossible== past that. A 30-stop delivery route and a 300-driver fleet running that route concurrently decide whether we need exact solving, heuristics, or a managed solver service.

#### Q: Do new orders need to be incorporated into a route the driver has already started, or only planned before the driver leaves the depot?
*Why it matters:* Static, pre-departure planning is a **batch problem** solvable in minutes with a slower, higher-quality algorithm. Mid-route re-optimization is a **real-time problem** that needs a fast heuristic that returns in well under a second, since the driver is waiting on their next turn-by-turn instruction.

#### Q: Are there hard constraints beyond distance, like delivery time windows, vehicle capacity, or driver shift-end times?
*Why it matters:* Pure shortest-path TSP is already hard; adding time windows and capacity turns this into a Vehicle Routing Problem with constraints, which needs a fundamentally different class of solver (constraint-aware heuristics, not plain nearest-neighbor).

#### Q: How accurate does drive-time estimation between two stops need to be: straight-line distance, or real road network and live traffic?
*Why it matters:* Straight-line distance is nearly free to compute but can be badly wrong in a city with rivers, highways, and one-way streets. Real routing-graph distances with live traffic are far more accurate but require calling (or hosting) a full routing engine for every pair of stops being considered, which is the dominant cost in the whole system.

### Functional Requirements
- Given a driver's list of assigned delivery stops, compute an ordered route minimizing total drive time.
- Support hard constraints: delivery time windows and vehicle capacity limits.
- Re-optimize the remaining, not-yet-visited portion of an in-progress route when a new stop is added.
- Provide turn-by-turn navigation for the currently active leg of the route.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Initial route planning for a full day's stops should complete in at most a few seconds per driver, even at 50+ stops.
- Mid-route re-optimization must return in under a second, since the driver is stopped or slowing down waiting for the next instruction.
- The system must scale to optimizing thousands of drivers' routes concurrently, especially during a morning dispatch rush.
- A returned route must always be valid (respects time windows and capacity) even if it isn't the mathematically optimal one; a slightly-suboptimal-but-correct route beats an optimal-but-late computation.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Exact solve cost at 40 stops:** Held-Karp dynamic programming is O(n^2 * 2^n): 40^2 * 2^40 ≈ 1,600 * 1.1 trillion ≈ 1.76 quadrillion operations, wildly infeasible for a single route, let alone 50,000 of them
- **Heuristic solve cost at 40 stops:** Nearest-neighbor construction is O(n^2) = 1,600 operations; a 2-opt improvement pass adds roughly O(n^2) per iteration, so even 50 iterations is 80,000 operations, comfortably sub-millisecond per route
- **Daily route computations across the fleet:** 50,000 drivers * 4 computations/day (1 initial + 3 re-optimizations) = 200,000 route computations/day ≈ 2.3/sec average, but concentrated in a morning dispatch spike of maybe 50x that
- **Dispatch-rush peak load:** 50,000 initial routes computed within a 10-minute dispatch window ≈ 83 routes/sec, each needing roughly 40x40 distance-matrix lookups (1,600 pairs), so a distance/ETA service must sustain over 100,000 pairwise lookups/sec at peak

*Summary:* The single fact driving this architecture is that **exact optimal solving** is computationally impossible at real fleet scale (a quadrillion operations for one 40-stop route), which forces every design decision toward fast **approximate heuristics**, and the resulting bottleneck moves from 'solving the route' to ==fetching enough accurate pairwise drive-time estimates fast enough to feed the solver==.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
The Traveling Salesman Problem is **NP-hard**. Held-Karp dynamic programming finds the exact optimal tour in **O(n^2 * 2^n)** time, which is only practical up to roughly 15-20 stops before it becomes ==computationally infeasible==, as the capacity math shows. Real delivery routes regularly have 30-100+ stops. Heuristics like **nearest-neighbor construction** followed by **2-opt** or Or-opt local search find a tour that's typically within 5-10% of optimal, in polynomial time, fast enough to run repeatedly throughout the day.

#### undefined
When a new order needs to be inserted into a route the driver is already executing, the system could throw away the whole plan and re-solve from scratch including already-completed stops, or it could keep completed stops fixed and only re-optimize the ordering of the **remaining, not-yet-visited stops** plus the new one.

lesson.content:
## Design Twitter

> **Core Concept:** The entire hard part of Twitter is the timeline, not the tweet: a celebrity with 100 million followers turns 'write one tweet' into a **fan-out** problem of enormous scale, and every real design decision here is about ==when that fan-out actually happens==.

### Problem Statement
Design a simplified version of Twitter: users can post short text messages
("tweets"), follow other users, and see a home timeline showing recent
tweets from everyone they follow, in roughly reverse-chronological order.
Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the follower distribution like? Are there celebrity accounts with tens of millions of followers?
*Why it matters:* A uniform 'everyone has ~200 followers' system and a system with Justin Bieber-scale accounts need completely different timeline architectures. This single fact decides the entire **feed-generation strategy**.

#### Q: Does the timeline need to be perfectly real-time, or is a few seconds of staleness acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Perfect real-time ordering across a distributed system is expensive. A few seconds of ==eventual consistency== opens up much cheaper, much more scalable designs.

#### Q: Do we need to support search, retweets, likes, and media (images/video), or just the core post-and-follow-and-read loop?
*Why it matters:* Each of those is close to its own system design problem. Scoping them out lets the interview focus on the genuinely hard part: timeline generation at scale.

#### Q: Should the timeline be pure reverse-chronological, or does it need ranking/relevance scoring?
*Why it matters:* Chronological is a well-understood fan-out problem. Ranked feeds add a whole separate scoring/ML layer on top, which is a materially different (and harder) system.

### Functional Requirements
- A user can post a tweet (short text, optionally with media).
- A user can follow and unfollow other users.
- A user can view their home timeline: recent tweets from everyone they follow, newest first.
- A user can view another user's profile timeline: just that user's own tweets.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- Reading a home timeline must be fast, well under a second, since it's the single most-loaded page in the entire product.
- The system must tolerate extreme skew in follower counts, from zero followers to tens of millions, without the celebrity accounts degrading the experience for everyone else.
- High availability for reads: a user should always be able to see some timeline, even if it's a few seconds stale, rather than see an error.
- Eventual consistency is acceptable: a followed user's new tweet can take a few seconds to appear in a follower's timeline.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Tweets written per day:** 200,000,000 / 2 = 100 million tweets/day ≈ 1,160 writes/sec average, low compared to reads
- **Timeline reads per day:** 200,000,000 * 5 = 1 billion reads/day ≈ 11,600 reads/sec average, and far higher at peak hours
- **Fan-out writes for an average tweet:** 1 tweet * 200 average followers = 200 fan-out writes; totally fine to do per-tweet
- **Fan-out writes for a celebrity tweet:** 1 tweet * 50,000,000 followers = 50 million fan-out writes for a single post, which is the number that breaks a naive design

*Summary:* This is a **read-heavy system** overall (roughly 10:1 reads to writes), but the real danger isn't the average case, it's the ==extreme skew==: a single celebrity tweet can demand more fan-out work than the rest of the platform combined, which is why timeline generation strategy is the entire design problem.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Fan-out on write means: when a tweet is posted, immediately push it into the pre-computed timeline of every follower. Reads become trivial (just read your own pre-built list), but a single celebrity tweet triggers tens of millions of writes at once. Fan-out on read means: store nothing extra at write time, and when a user opens their timeline, pull recent tweets live from everyone they follow and merge them on the fly. Writes stay cheap regardless of follower count, but reads become expensive, since a user follows hundreds of people and each read has to fan out across all of them.

#### undefined
The timeline_cache for a user doesn't need to store their entire history, just enough recent tweet IDs to serve the first several pages (say, the most recent 800 tweet IDs). Older entries can be trimmed on write, and if a user scrolls back further than what's cached, that older portion falls back to a live, more expensive read, which is rare enough in practice to be acceptable.

#### undefined
A naive auto-increment ID needs a single source of truth, which becomes a write bottleneck at this scale. A Snowflake-style ID (timestamp bits + machine/shard ID bits + a per-machine sequence number, packed into a 64-bit integer) lets every app server generate globally unique, roughly time-sortable IDs independently, with no coordination needed between servers at all.

## Design Discord

> **Core Concept:** Discord is really two different real-time systems wearing one UI: **durable, ordered text messaging** per channel, and ==lossy, latency-obsessed voice transport== per channel, and the entire architecture is about keeping those two very different delivery models from being forced through the same pipe.

### Problem Statement
Design a system like Discord: users organize into servers (communities),
each server contains multiple text and voice channels, members can send
persistent text messages per channel and join low-latency live voice
calls per channel, and servers have a role-based permission system
controlling who can do what. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Are text and voice genuinely separate subsystems, or does the design need to unify them into a single message/event pipeline?

## Design a Distributed Cache System (like Redis/Memcached itself)

> **Core Concept:** Building the cache itself flips the usual framing: instead of asking how to use a cache, the whole design is about how to spread keys across many memory-bound nodes so any one node's failure or overload doesn't take out the whole cache, which makes **consistent hashing** and replication, not the get/set API, the actual core of the system.

### Problem Statement
Design the cache service itself, not a system that happens to use a cache
in front of a database, but the distributed in-memory key-value store
that other systems would plug in as their cache layer. It needs to store
key-value pairs in memory across many nodes, evict data intelligently
when full, survive individual node failures without losing all cached
data, and let clients find the right node for a given key quickly.
Design it.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Is this a pure look-aside cache (best-effort, losing data is tolerable) or does it need durability guarantees (data must survive a node crash)?
*Why it matters:* A pure best-effort cache can treat node failure as 'those keys are just gone, refetch from the source of truth,' which is much simpler. Requiring durability means adding replication (and the consistency trade-offs that come with it), a materially bigger system.

#### Q: What eviction policy is expected when a node runs out of memory: LRU, LFU, or TTL-based expiry, or some combination?
*Why it matters:* This decides what per-key metadata every node must track (last-access time for LRU, access frequency for LFU, expiry timestamps for TTL) and directly affects memory overhead per entry, which matters a lot at cache scale.

#### Q: How many nodes are expected, and how often do nodes get added or removed (scaling events, failures)?
*Why it matters:* Frequent membership changes make the key-to-node mapping scheme matter enormously: a naive mod-N hashing scheme would remap almost every key on every node change, causing a massive cache-miss storm each time, which is exactly what consistent hashing is designed to prevent.

#### Q: What's the acceptable data-loss window if a node fails: zero (synchronous replication), or a few seconds (asynchronous replication) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Synchronous replication to a replica before acknowledging a write guarantees no loss but adds latency to every write. Asynchronous replication is faster but accepts a small window where a crash loses the most recent writes, a real trade-off that has to be chosen deliberately, not defaulted into.

### Functional Requirements
- Support basic key-value operations: GET, SET, DELETE, with optional TTL (time-to-live) on a key.
- Distribute keys across many cache nodes so no single node has to hold the entire dataset.
- Evict keys automatically under memory pressure according to a defined policy (e.g. LRU).
- Continue serving most of the dataset correctly when any single node fails, not lose the entire cache.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- GET and SET operations must be extremely low latency, sub-millisecond, since the entire point of a cache is to be faster than the system behind it.
- The system must scale horizontally: adding nodes should increase total capacity and throughput close to linearly, not require a full redistribution of every key.
- The system must tolerate individual node failure gracefully, with a bounded, small amount of data loss or unavailability, not a total outage.
- Memory usage per node must stay predictable and boundable, so operators can provision capacity confidently rather than guessing.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Minimum node count for capacity:** 2,000 GB / 64 GB per node ≈ 32 nodes minimum just to fit the dataset in memory, before accounting for replication overhead
- **Node count with replication:** With 1 replica per key (2x storage for durability), effective capacity need doubles to ~4,000 GB / 64 GB ≈ 63 nodes, this replication overhead is a real, first-class cost of the durability requirement, not free
- **Per-node throughput requirement:** 2,000,000 ops/sec / 63 nodes ≈ 31,750 ops/sec/node average, well within what a single well-provisioned in-memory node can serve (in-memory ops typically handle 100,000+/sec), so throughput is not the binding constraint here, memory capacity and replication are
- **Total key count:** 2 TB / 1 KB per entry ≈ 2 billion keys, which is the number that determines how large the consistent-hashing ring's virtual-node metadata and node-lookup structures need to be, and confirms a single node's in-memory hash table (millions to tens of millions of keys) could never hold this alone

*Summary:* The number that actually drives this design is not raw throughput, which one in-memory node handles easily, it's that fitting 2 TB (4 TB once replicated) of hot data in RAM requires spreading it across dozens of nodes, which is why the key-to-node mapping (consistent hashing) and what happens when that mapping changes are the entire hard problem, not the get/set operations themselves.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
The naive approach, hash(key) mod N where N is the node count, is simple but catastrophic on any membership change: adding or removing even one node changes N, which changes the mod result for nearly every key, remapping almost the entire keyspace at once and causing a massive wave of cache misses as every client suddenly looks in the wrong place. Consistent hashing solves this by hashing both keys and nodes onto the same fixed-size ring; adding or removing a node only affects the keys between that node and its immediate neighbor on the ring, a small fraction of the total keyspace, not everything.

#### undefined
In a pure single-copy cache, a node failure simply erases every key that node owned, which downstream systems must treat as a mass cache miss and refetch from the source of truth, a legitimate design if the source of truth can absorb that spike. If durability matters more, each key is also written to one or more replica nodes (typically the next node(s) clockwise on the hash ring), so when the primary node for a key fails, a replica already has the data and can be promoted, with only a brief window of unavailability during failure detection and promotion, not full data loss.

## Design a Distributed Database (from Scratch, General)

> **Core Concept:** A single machine gives you consistency, availability, and simplicity for free; the moment you spread data across a network, **CAP theorem** forces you to give up availability or consistency during a partition, and every other decision in this design, how you shard, how you replicate, how you commit a transaction, is really just a consequence of which side of that trade-off you deliberately chose.

### Problem Statement
Design a distributed database from scratch: a system that stores data
across many machines, supports reads and writes with a chosen consistency
guarantee, survives individual node failures without losing committed
data, and can execute transactions that span multiple partitions of data.
Design the storage and coordination layers end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need strong (linearizable) consistency, or is eventual/causal consistency acceptable for this workload?
*Why it matters:* This is the single decision CAP theorem forces explicitly: under a network partition, a strongly consistent system must ==refuse some requests== to avoid returning stale or conflicting data, while an eventually consistent one stays available and reconciles later. It determines the replication protocol, the read path, and the failure behavior for the entire system.

#### Q: Do transactions need to span multiple shards/partitions, or is single-shard (single-key or single-partition) atomicity enough?
*Why it matters:* Single-shard transactions are cheap, a partition can just use a local lock and a write-ahead log. Cross-shard transactions require **distributed coordination** (two-phase commit or a similar protocol), which adds real latency and a whole new failure mode: a coordinator crashing mid-commit.

#### Q: What's the read/write ratio, and how large is the dataset relative to what a single node could hold?
*Why it matters:* If the data fits on one beefy machine, partitioning is unnecessary complexity. Partitioning only earns its cost once the dataset or the write throughput genuinely exceeds one machine's capacity, which is the actual justification for sharding at all.

#### Q: What failure modes must we tolerate: single node crashes, whole rack/datacenter loss, or network partitions between regions?
*Why it matters:* Tolerating a single node crash needs only local replication (a handful of replicas in one datacenter). Tolerating a full datacenter loss needs geo-replication across regions, which multiplies write latency because a majority of geographically distant replicas must acknowledge every write.

### Functional Requirements
- Clients can read and write individual keys/rows, with data distributed (sharded) across many nodes.
- The system replicates every piece of data onto multiple nodes so a single node failure doesn't lose or block access to data.
- The system supports transactions that atomically read and write multiple keys, including keys on different shards.
- The system detects and recovers from node failure automatically, promoting a replica to take over without operator intervention.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- The system must survive the loss of any single node (and ideally a whole availability zone) without ==losing any committed write==.
- The system must state and hold to an explicit **consistency model** (e.g. linearizable, or bounded-staleness) rather than leaving it ambiguous, since every client-facing guarantee depends on it.
- Write latency for a cross-shard transaction must stay bounded (low tens of milliseconds within one region) even though it requires coordination across multiple nodes.
- The system must scale horizontally: adding nodes should increase both storage capacity and write throughput roughly linearly, not require a full re-architecture.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Total data with replication:** 100 TB * 3 replicas = 300 TB of total stored bytes at the two-year mark
- **Shard count and size:** Target ~50 GB per shard for manageable rebalancing and recovery time: 100 TB / 50 GB = 2,000 shards, each replicated 3x = 6,000 shard-replicas to place across the cluster
- **Write throughput per shard:** 50,000 writes/sec / 2,000 shards = 25 writes/sec/shard average, comfortably low per shard even though the aggregate is high, confirming sharding by key range/hash successfully spreads load
- **Cross-shard transaction volume:** 50,000 writes/sec * 10% = **5,000 cross-shard transactions/sec**, each needing coordination across ~3 shards, meaning ~15,000 extra inter-node coordination messages/sec just for distributed commit

*Summary:* The dominant scaling driver isn't raw data volume, 300 TB spread over 2,000 shards is unremarkable, it's the 5,000/sec cross-shard transactions, since each one requires multi-node coordination (not just a local write), and that ==coordination cost==, not storage or single-shard throughput, is what determines the system's actual write latency and ceiling.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
**Range-based sharding** assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (e.g. keys 'a' through 'm' on shard 1), which keeps related, sequentially-accessed keys together and makes range scans (e.g. 'all orders from this week') cheap, hitting few shards. **Hash-based sharding** assigns a shard by hashing the key, spreading logically related keys uniformly at random across shards, which avoids hot shards from sequential access patterns (like monotonically increasing IDs all landing on the newest range) but makes range scans expensive, since a scan now has to fan out to nearly every shard.

#### undefined
CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between **Consistency** (every read sees the latest committed write, but some requests may be refused/blocked) and **Availability** (every request gets a response, but it might be stale). A linearizable system (like this design's default, using consensus per shard) picks consistency: if a shard's replica group can't reach a majority (a partition isolates the minority), the minority side ==stops serving writes, and even reads==, rather than risk returning stale data. An eventually consistent system picks availability: every replica keeps serving reads and writes even when partitioned, and conflicting writes are reconciled later (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs).

#### undefined
Two-phase commit has a **prepare phase** (the coordinator asks every participating shard to lock the relevant keys, persist an intent, and vote yes/no) and a **commit phase** (once every participant votes yes, the coordinator tells all of them to commit; if any votes no, it tells all of them to abort). The mechanism is straightforward; the actual hard problem is ==coordinator failure==: if the coordinator crashes after some shards have prepared (locked and voted yes) but before it sends the final commit/abort decision, those shards are stuck holding locks indefinitely, unable to unilaterally decide whether to commit or abort, since only the coordinator knew the collective outcome.

#### Q: What failure modes must we tolerate: single node crashes, whole rack/datacenter loss, or network partitions between regions?
*Why it matters:* Tolerating a single node crash needs only local replication (a handful of replicas in one datacenter). Tolerating a full datacenter loss needs geo-replication across regions, which multiplies write latency because a majority of geographically distant replicas must acknowledge every write.

### Functional Requirements
- Clients can read and write individual keys/rows, with data distributed (sharded) across many nodes.
- The system replicates every piece of data onto multiple nodes so a single node failure doesn't lose or block access to data.
- The system supports transactions that atomically read and write multiple keys, including keys on different shards.
- The system detects and recovers from node failure automatically, promoting a replica to take over without operator intervention.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- The system must survive the loss of any single node (and ideally a whole availability zone) without ==losing any committed write==.
- The system must state and hold to an explicit **consistency model** (e.g. linearizable, or bounded-staleness) rather than leaving it ambiguous, since every client-facing guarantee depends on it.
- Write latency for a cross-shard transaction must stay bounded (low tens of milliseconds within one region) even though it requires coordination across multiple nodes.
- The system must scale horizontally: adding nodes should increase both storage capacity and write throughput roughly linearly, not require a full re-architecture.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Total data with replication:** 100 TB * 3 replicas = 300 TB of total stored bytes at the two-year mark
- **Shard count and size:** Target ~50 GB per shard for manageable rebalancing and recovery time: 100 TB / 50 GB = 2,000 shards, each replicated 3x = 6,000 shard-replicas to place across the cluster
- **Write throughput per shard:** 50,000 writes/sec / 2,000 shards = 25 writes/sec/shard average, comfortably low per shard even though the aggregate is high, confirming sharding by key range/hash successfully spreads load
- **Cross-shard transaction volume:** 50,000 writes/sec * 10% = **5,000 cross-shard transactions/sec**, each needing coordination across ~3 shards, meaning ~15,000 extra inter-node coordination messages/sec just for distributed commit

*Summary:* The dominant scaling driver isn't raw data volume, 300 TB spread over 2,000 shards is unremarkable, it's the 5,000/sec cross-shard transactions, since each one requires multi-node coordination (not just a local write), and that ==coordination cost==, not storage or single-shard throughput, is what determines the system's actual write latency and ceiling.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
**Range-based sharding** assigns contiguous key ranges to shards (e.g. keys 'a' through 'm' on shard 1), which keeps related, sequentially-accessed keys together and makes range scans (e.g. 'all orders from this week') cheap, hitting few shards. **Hash-based sharding** assigns a shard by hashing the key, spreading logically related keys uniformly at random across shards, which avoids hot shards from sequential access patterns (like monotonically increasing IDs all landing on the newest range) but makes range scans expensive, since a scan now has to fan out to nearly every shard.

#### undefined
CAP theorem says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between **Consistency** (every read sees the latest committed write, but some requests may be refused/blocked) and **Availability** (every request gets a response, but it might be stale). A linearizable system (like this design's default, using consensus per shard) picks consistency: if a shard's replica group can't reach a majority (a partition isolates the minority), the minority side ==stops serving writes, and even reads==, rather than risk returning stale data. An eventually consistent system picks availability: every replica keeps serving reads and writes even when partitioned, and conflicting writes are reconciled later (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs).

#### undefined
Two-phase commit has a **prepare phase** (the coordinator asks every participating shard to lock the relevant keys, persist an intent, and vote yes/no) and a **commit phase** (once every participant votes yes, the coordinator tells all of them to commit; if any votes no, it tells all of them to abort). The mechanism is straightforward; the actual hard problem is ==coordinator failure==: if the coordinator crashes after some shards have prepared (locked and voted yes) but before it sends the final commit/abort decision, those shards are stuck holding locks indefinitely, unable to unilaterally decide whether to commit or abort, since only the coordinator knew the collective outcome.

callout.title: Engineering Principle
callout.text: A single machine gives you consistency, availability, and simplicity for free; the moment you spread data across a network, **CAP theorem** forces you to give up availability or consistency during a partition, and every other decision in this design, how you shard, how you replicate, how you commit a transaction, is really just a consequence of which side of that trade-off you deliberately chose.

## Design a Distributed File System (GFS/HDFS-style)

> **Core Concept:** A single machine tracking where every piece of data lives, while none of the data itself passes through that machine, is not a contradiction, it's the whole architecture: keeping **metadata tiny and centralized** is exactly what lets the actual bytes scale out to thousands of machines with no coordination between them.

### Problem Statement
Design a distributed file system that can store files far larger than any
single disk, spread across thousands of commodity machines, for large
batch-processing workloads (think: the storage layer under a MapReduce or
Spark cluster). Files are mostly written once and read many times, often
sequentially, in large chunks. Design the system end to end.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Is this optimized for large sequential reads over huge files, or for lots of small random-access reads and writes?
*Why it matters:* GFS/HDFS-style systems are built for the former: batch analytics over huge append-mostly files. Small random writes and low-latency point lookups are a fundamentally different workload (that's what a database or key-value store is for), and designing for the wrong one produces the wrong system entirely.

#### Q: How many machines and how much total data are we targeting, and what's an acceptable rate of individual machine failure?
*Why it matters:* At thousands of commodity machines, disk and machine failure isn't an edge case, it's a ==daily occurrence==. That single fact is what forces **replication** and automatic re-replication into the design from day one, rather than treating failure as exceptional.

#### Q: Do files need to support concurrent appends from multiple writers, or is single-writer-at-a-time sufficient?
*Why it matters:* Concurrent appends (many workers logging into the same file simultaneously) need a specific atomic record-append protocol. If writes are always single-writer, the write path can be much simpler.

#### Q: Is strong consistency required on every read immediately after a write, or is a brief window of staleness acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Chunk replication is asynchronous by default for throughput. Requiring every replica to be immediately consistent on every write adds real latency and coordination cost that a batch-analytics workload usually doesn't need.

### Functional Requirements
- A client can create, write (including append), and read files that may be far larger than any single machine's disk.
- Files are automatically split into fixed-size chunks and distributed across many chunkservers.
- The system automatically maintains a configured replication factor for every chunk, even as machines fail.
- A client can list a directory and look up which chunkservers hold the chunks of a given file.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- High throughput for large, mostly-sequential reads and writes must dominate over low-latency for small random operations, which this system does not optimize for.
- The system must keep operating correctly and without data loss through continuous, routine hardware failure of individual disks and machines.
- The system must scale to thousands of machines and petabytes of data without the metadata layer becoming the bottleneck.
- Re-replication after a chunkserver failure must happen automatically and quickly enough that a second failure during the repair window doesn't cause permanent data loss.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Usable data capacity after replication:** 240 PB raw / 3 replicas = 80 PB of actual distinct file data storable across the cluster
- **Number of files the cluster can hold:** 80 PB / 500 MB average file size = 80,000,000,000,000,000 bytes / 500,000,000 bytes ≈ 160 million files
- **Chunks per average file, and total chunks in the cluster:** 500 MB / 64 MB ≈ 8 chunks per average file; 160 million files * 8 chunks ≈ 1.28 billion chunks, and with replication, 1.28 billion * 3 ≈ 3.84 billion chunk replicas placed across chunkservers
- **Metadata size held in memory by the single master:** Roughly 64 bytes of metadata per chunk (id, version, replica locations) * 1.28 billion chunks ≈ 82 GB, which fits comfortably in RAM on one modern machine, this is the number that makes a single-master design viable at all

*Summary:* The number that makes or breaks this whole design is **metadata-per-chunk**, not total bytes stored: because a large fixed chunk size keeps the chunk count (and therefore the master's in-memory metadata) small relative to petabytes of actual data, a single machine can hold the entire cluster's metadata in RAM, which is precisely what lets the master stay a simple, non-sharded single point of coordination instead of becoming the bottleneck.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
Keeping exactly one master (rather than sharding metadata across many machines) makes the design vastly simpler to reason about: there's one place that decides chunk placement, one place that serializes namespace mutations, no distributed-metadata-consensus problem to solve. The catch is that the master must never become the bottleneck for actual data transfer (which it doesn't, since data flows client-to-chunkserver directly), and it is a single point of failure for the whole cluster unless it's specifically hardened.

#### undefined
A tiny chunk size means a huge number of chunks for the same total data, which blows up the master's metadata (more chunks to track) and means every large sequential read has to negotiate with the master and possibly many different chunkservers for tiny pieces. A huge chunk size means fewer chunks and less metadata, but small files waste space (internal fragmentation) and, more importantly, a small number of very hot files can concentrate too much load onto too few chunkservers. ==64 MB is a deliberate middle point==: large enough to keep metadata small and let a client do one lookup then stream a large sequential read from one chunkserver, small enough that a busy file's chunks still spread across multiple machines.

#### undefined
The master detects a dead chunkserver purely through missed heartbeats (no heartbeat within a timeout, typically tens of seconds), at which point every chunk that server held drops below its target replication factor. The master doesn't reactively fix this one chunk at a time; it maintains a priority queue of under-replicated chunks across the whole cluster and continuously assigns re-replication work to other chunkservers, prioritizing chunks with the fewest remaining replicas (a chunk down to zero replicas, i.e. data loss, is the highest priority of all, though ideally that never happens because re-replication finishes before a second failure).

## Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator

> **Core Concept:** A distributed ID generator exists because uniqueness is easy on one machine and hard across a thousand, so the whole design is about encoding just enough shared context (time and machine identity) into each ID that no two machines ever need to talk to each other to guarantee they **won't collide**.

### Problem Statement
Design a service that generates unique IDs for rows/records (like tweets,
orders, or comments) across a large, horizontally sharded system. IDs must
be unique across every shard and server, generated with very low latency,
and ideally roughly sortable by creation time. Design how this ID
generation actually works.


### Clarifying Questions & Trade-offs
#### Q: Do IDs need to be roughly sortable by creation time, or is pure uniqueness enough?
*Why it matters:* Time-sortable IDs make range queries and pagination ('give me the next page of newest items') trivial with an index. Pure random uniqueness (like a UUID) doesn't sort meaningfully, which pushes sorting work onto a separate index or timestamp column.

#### Q: How many ID-generating machines/services will there be, and how many IDs per second does the system need at peak?
*Why it matters:* This decides how many bits need to be reserved for machine/worker identity versus sequence number within a fixed-size ID (commonly 64 bits total), which is a real budget that has to be planned, not assumed.

#### Q: Can we tolerate a centralized ID service, or does generation need to happen with zero coordination between machines?
*Why it matters:* A single centralized counter service is simple and perfectly ordered but becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure at high write volume. A decentralized scheme (like Snowflake) needs no coordination per ID, at the cost of only approximate time-ordering and needing careful clock handling.

#### Q: What happens if a machine's clock drifts backward (NTP correction, VM migration) mid-operation?
*Why it matters:* Any scheme that embeds a timestamp in the ID can generate a duplicate or out-of-order ID if the clock that generated it moves backward before the next ID is requested. This has to be handled explicitly, not assumed away.

### Functional Requirements
- Generate IDs that are unique across every machine and shard in the system, with no coordination required per ID.
- IDs should be roughly sortable by creation time, so a newer ID is numerically larger than an older one.
- Support at least tens of thousands of ID generations per second per machine, with many machines generating concurrently.
- IDs should fit in a standard 64-bit integer for efficient storage and indexing.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- ID generation must be extremely low latency, effectively local, since it happens on the hot path of every single write.
- The system must have no single point of failure: losing one machine should not stop any other machine from generating valid, unique IDs.
- The scheme must tolerate reasonable clock skew or drift between machines without producing duplicate IDs.
- The ID space must be large enough not to exhaust for decades of expected write volume.

### Capacity Estimation
- **Per-machine ID rate needed:** 500,000 IDs/sec / 1,000 machines = 500 IDs/sec/machine average, but a single machine must handle bursts well above that, so the sequence-number space per millisecond needs headroom, not just the average
- **Bit budget: timestamp:** 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch gives 2^41 ≈ 2.2 trillion ms ≈ about 69 years of range, comfortably covering the 50-year requirement
- **Bit budget: machine/worker ID:** 10 bits gives 2^10 = 1,024 distinct machine IDs, enough for the 1,000 app servers with a little headroom to grow
- **Bit budget: sequence number:** 12 bits gives 2^12 = 4,096 unique IDs per machine per millisecond, i.e. up to 4,096,000 IDs/sec/machine, far above the 500/sec/machine average and comfortably above realistic bursts

*Summary:* The number that actually drives this design is not the total throughput, which is easily achievable, it's that a single 64-bit integer has to be split into timestamp, machine ID, and sequence bits that all fit together, and once that split is fixed (41/10/12 here), every other property (69-year lifespan, 1,024 machines, 4,096 IDs/ms/machine) falls out of that one decision.

### Deep Dives
#### undefined
A traditional auto-increment primary key is trivial on a single database, the database itself guarantees uniqueness and ordering. The moment the database is sharded across multiple machines, auto-increment breaks: each shard's own auto-increment would produce colliding IDs (shard A's row 500 and shard B's row 500 are not the same row). Snowflake-style IDs solve this by moving uniqueness generation out of the database entirely and into the application layer, encoding machine identity directly into the ID so no two machines can ever produce the same value, without either machine needing to know the other exists.

#### undefined
If NTP corrects a machine's clock backward, or a VM is paused and resumed, that machine could generate an ID with an earlier timestamp than an ID it already generated moments before, which risks either an ordering violation or, worse, an actual collision if the sequence counter also happens to repeat. The standard mitigation is for the ID generator to track the last timestamp it used; if the current clock reading is earlier than that, the generator refuses to issue new IDs (or waits) until the clock catches back up past the last used timestamp, trading brief unavailability of ID generation on that one machine for a hard uniqueness guarantee.
